profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.

summary_quotes.text: Blank Bio is excited to release Ladon, a transcriptomic foundation model trained on millions of bulk RNAseq samples.
It is pre-trained with masked token reconstruction on isoform-level sequences
The labeled data is then used to adapt Ladon to clinical tasks such as predicting survival, recurrence, and treatment response.
An RNA model for patients is therefore only as useful as its accuracy in cohorts it was never fit on.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.
sections.source_locator: Report page 2, Introducing Ladon; page 11, Methods: Ladon representations; page 6; page 28, Methods

quotes.text: Ladon is a 3-billion-parameter transformer encoder-decoder trained on millions of bulk RNA-seq samples.
Because the objective is selfsupervised, Ladon learns from every sample, not just the small fraction with outcome labels.

We perform supervised mid-training to predict patient and tumor characteristics, including disease stage, age, tumor grade and genomic alterations, alongside other clinical outcomes. We then discard the prediction heads and keep the encoder fixed, fitting downstream outcome predictors on the resulting embeddings.
We fit a linear Cox survival model on Ladon's fixed representations of one cohort and apply it unchanged to the other.

sections.title: Evaluation in the report
sections.body: Every result is reported on a setting not used for fitting: a held-out trial, another cohort or another platform. Survival models fitted on TCGA were applied unchanged to CPTAC and the reverse; the developers report Ladon ahead of differential gene expression signatures, BulkRNABERT and BulkFormer, and that adding Ladon to clinical covariates improved survival prediction in all 12 target cohorts. They also report better response prediction for immunotherapy than PD-L1 expression, recovery of isoform usage from gene-level counts (median Pearson r of 0.81 across 3,000 genes in held-out tumours), and cell-composition inference from single-cell references. For the scaling claim they assembled their own patient-level benchmark, ClinBench, aggregating 142 tasks across survival, treatment response and patient and tumour characteristics, and report that lower pretraining reconstruction loss went with better average performance on it, with reconstruction loss still falling at the largest size tested. All of these are the developers' own results in an unreviewed report.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Millions of bulk RNA-seq samples; the corpus, its sources and sample count are not listed. Short-read isoform estimates were used. Supervised mid-training uses disease stage, age, tumour grade, genomic alterations and clinical outcomes; TCGA and CPTAC outcome labels were kept out of the encoder supervision. For the labelled part the report is more specific: survival predictors were fitted on up to 1,000 indication-matched samples, then about 8,000 across all eligible TCGA projects, then about 18,000 with non-trial cohorts and other trials added, and the immunotherapy response classifier used a context of 1,419 patients from 33 academic cohorts.
